
## Methods

The analysis pipeline is summarised in @fig-pipeline.

![Schematic analysis pipeline.](figures/chapter2/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline height="60%" column="page"}

### Intracranial data

The intracranial EEG data come from the MNI Open iEEG Atlas [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial], a normative resource compiled from 106 patients with refractory epilepsy recorded at three centres. Only channels implanted in brain regions that were determined to be non-epileptogenic throughout the monitoring period were retained, yielding 1772 channels (13 channels were removed from intitial release as were later judged erroneus on visual inspection) distributed across 38 cortical regions defined by the MICCAI atlas. @fig-frauscher-atlas shows the channel coverage, distinguishing depth/stereo-EEG contacts from cortical grid and strip contacts across both hemispheres.

The 38 regions were built by consolidating 20 smaller MICCAI labels into 8 functional groups so that each region held at least 5 channels, while 16 labels were omitted due to lack of coverage. For each channel, 60 seconds of resting wakefulness data with eyes closed were available.
 The atlas authors resampled the signals to 200 Hz, applied an 80 Hz low-pass antialiasing filter, and reduced power-line interference with an adaptive filter.


### Source-reconstructed HD-EEG

Five minutes  of eyes-open resting state EEG data were collected in 19 healthy young adult volunteers (age $28\pm 6$ years, 14 females) with Ethics Committee of ETH Zurich approval. EEG signals were recorded at 1000Hz sampling rate using a 256channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net by Electrical Geodesics (Eugene, Oregon, USA). HD-EEG data were recorded with eyes open condition.
The full details of collecting and preprocessing this dataset dataset were described in @samogin2019SharedConnectionspecificIntrinsic and  @samogin2020FrequencydependentFunctionalConnectivity.  The poor  chanels were  identified (0-13 pers subject) and interpolated, data was band-pass filtered within 1-80Hz range and biological artifact were removed using fixed-point ICA (FastICA) algorithm. The realistic head model was provided as input to the exact low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (eLORETA) algorithm [@pascual-marqui2011AssessingInteractionsBrain], together with the  preprocessed EEG signals, to estimate brain activity in the source space at high-temporal resolution.

 The  following steps and timeseries extraction were chosen to  matche the iEEG atlas: source activity was extracted from reconstructed sources  using average coordinates from the  electrodes within 76 MICCAI-defined ROIs in MNI space,  resulting in 1444 virtual sensors, with the grouped regional reference coordinates illustrated in Figure @fig-frauscher-atlas, panel B.

(**A**) Glass-brain visualization of the 1785 intracranial EEG channels, with depth and stereo-EEG contacts shown in blue and cortical grid/strip contacts shown in orange. For visualization, left-hemisphere channel coordinates were assigned negative x-values based on the hemisphere label. ### Common spectral processing

 
 In ieeg dataset power spectral density (PSD) was estimated using Welch's method with 2-second Hamming windows and 50% overlap, resulting in a frequency resolution of 0.5 Hz.  Full preprocessing details are given in @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.

In HD EEG reconstucted sesnors, 60s activity was extracted  from each time series according to the parameters defined in Frauscher's paper (sampling frequency 200Hz). Spectral densities were computed using identical Welch parameters (2s windows, 50% overlap, 0.5 Hz resolution). 

All spectral data were normalized to unit total power to ensure that the comparison focused on the distribution of frequency peaks (e.g., the occipital alpha or hippocampal delta) rather than absolute amplitude differences between scalp and intracranial sensors.

Where later analyses use canonical bands, we define them as delta 1-4 Hz, theta 4-8 Hz, alpha 8-13 Hz, beta 13-30 Hz,  gamma 30-80 Hz. We use 1 Hz as the lower bound throughout to aid the cross-modal comparison.

###  Recovery of regional spectral organisation on uncorrected spectra

#### K-means clustering and no-peak reference 

For direct comparison with the original atlas, we followed the peak-detection procedure of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.
The normalised power spectra were classified into k groups using k-means with 160 features (0.5 Hz bins from 0.5 to 80 Hz), Euclidean distance, and 100 repetitions.  We increased $k$ until a group without peaks emerged, defined as the group whose mean normalised spectrum fell below the maximum among the other groups, and kept the 50% of channels closest to that group's mean as the no-peak set.

To test for the presence of region-specific peaks against this no-peak reference set, the spectrum was divided into frequency intervals. The data driven condition defined initially in @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial that  each bin contains at least 4% of total mean power brought different numbers of bins between modalities so we used interval intitially defined in the orginal paper and  the 160 frequency bins were grouped into 22 frequency intervals bbased on the condition that, yielding
boundaries at 0.5, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 3.25, 3.75, 4.25, 5.25, 6.25, 6.75, 7.75, 8.25, 9.25, 10.25, 11.75, 13.25, 15.25, 17.25, 20.25, 24.25, 31.75, and 80 Hz. 

We determined  the presence of a peak in a given frequency interval for a particular brain region by comparing the distribution of spectral densities of all channels in that region against the no-peak set, using a one-sided two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test at the 5% significance level with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons across 42 regions (38 cortical regions plus 4 lobes) and 22 frequency intervals (hemispheres grouped together).

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov screen identifies where a region differs from the no-peak set but not how many of its channels drive that difference. To quantify how widespread the effect was within the region each channel's relative power in that interval was compared against the no-peak distribution with a one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney U) test at the 5% level, uncorrected. We report the proportion of the region's channels that exceeded the no-peak set. This second stage mirrors the two-step logic of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial.

For the HD-EEG data we applied the same procedure and kept the iEEG-derived intervals for comparability, even though the 4% power condition did not hold for the source-reconstructed spectra; the consequences of this are reported in the Results.


#### Canonical-band relative-power map

As a second, complementary  approach, we mapped each region's normalised PSD onto the canonical bands defined above and took relative band power per region.

#### Cross-modal correspondence on uncorrected spectra

We quantified cross-modal agreement on the unit-power PSDs using the band-overlap metric of @afnan2024ValidationMEGSource. Channels were pooled across hemispheres by grouping on the hemisphere-agnostic MICCAI region name, collapsing left and right ROIs into the 38 bilateral regions of the atlas. Within each region $r$, we treated the iEEG atlas as the reference modality and the HD-EEG source data as the estimated modality. Let $\widetilde{L}_r(f)$ denote the median log-PSD across the channels of region $r$ at frequency bin $f$, and $\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)$ the corresponding HD-EEG standard deviation. The bin-wise overlap is

$$
\text{overlap}_r(f) =
\begin{cases}
    1 - \dfrac{\bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \bigr\rvert}
              {\text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f)},
        & \bigl\lvert \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{iEEG}}_r(f) - \widetilde{L}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \bigr\rvert
          \le \text{SD}^{\,\text{HD}}_r(f) \\[2mm]
    0,  & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$


The metric equals 1 when the iEEG median lands exactly on the HD-EEG median and falls linearly to 0 once the two medians differ by one HD-EEG standard deviation. We averaged the bin-wise overlap across the frequency bins of each canonical band, giving one value per region per band, and report both the bin-level and the band-averaged overlap. To complement the overlap, we also rank-correlated the regional band estimates between modalities across regions (Spearman).

### Spectral parametrisation

We asked whether separating periodic from aperiodic activity changes the above picture. We addressed it in two linked ways: by modelling oscillatory peaks directly with specparam, and by removing the aperiodic background and recomputing the cross-modal overlap.


#### specparam settings

PSDs were parameterised using specparam (formerly FOOOF; @donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower) with the following shared settings:

- Fitting frequency range: 1-80 Hz (primary); 1-45 Hz (range comparison
  in Section )
- Peak width limits: 1.0-8.0 Hz
- Maximum number of peaks: 8
- Minimum peak height: 0.1 (log power)
- Peak threshold: 3.0 standard deviations of the residual

Model fits were evaluated using R² and mean absolute error; fits with R² below 0.90 were flagged for inspection and the sensitivity of regional results to their inclusion or exclusion was assessed.


###  Aperiodic parametrisation and model selection

Two aperiodic models are used. In **fixed** mode the aperiodic component
is modelled in log-power space as

$$L_{\mathrm{ap}}(f) = b - \chi \cdot \log_{10}(f)$$

with offset $b$ and exponent $\chi$.. In **knee** mode,

$$L_{\mathrm{ap}}(f) = b - \log_{10}(k + f^{\chi})$$

with an additional knee parameter $k$.

We selected the aperiodic mode per modality by Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). Both modes are fit to every channel spectrum with identical peak settings and frequency range, and the two fits are compared on each spectrum. Following @ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses, the BIC of a single spectrum under the Gaussian model (Foygel and Drton 2010) is

$$\mathrm{BIC} = N \log(\mathrm{MSE}) + n_p \log(N),$$

where $N$ is the number of fitted frequency bins, MSE is the mean squared residual of the full model in log-power space (aperiodic plus all peaks; equivalently the square of specparam's RMSE error term), and $n_p$ is the number of free parameters. With up to eight peaks, $n_p = 3 n_{\mathrm{peaks}} + n_{\mathrm{ap}}$, where each peak contributes three parameters and $n_{\mathrm{ap}} = 2$ for the fixed model (offset, exponent) and $n_{\mathrm{ap}} = 3$ for the knee model (offset, knee, exponent). On the per-spectrum scale of Raftery (1995), as used by @ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses, an absolute BIC difference of 0--2 is weak evidence for the lower-BIC model, 2--6 is positive evidence, and above 6 is strong evidence.

@ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses apply this criterion per spectrum and do not prescribe how to choose a single mode for a set of spectra. We extend it as follows. The channel set is held fixed within each modality, so the fixed and knee fits are paired observations on the same spectra. Treating channel spectra as independent fits, the total BIC of applying one mode to the whole modality is the sum of the per-spectrum BICs, so the dataset-level criterion is the summed paired difference

$$\textstyle\sum_c \Delta\mathrm{BIC}_c = \sum_c \left(\mathrm{BIC}^{\mathrm{knee}}_c - \mathrm{BIC}^{\mathrm{fixed}}_c\right),$$

over channels $c$; the mode with the smaller total BIC (negative sum favouring knee, positive favouring fixed) is selected for that modality. Because a summed criterion can be dominated by a few spectra, we additionally report two robustness diagnostics that do not drive the choice: the fraction of channels individually favouring each mode, with each channel's evidence graded on the Raftery scale above, and the mean per-channel $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}$ with its 95% confidence interval (Section 3.2.1).

#### Per-band peak prevalence

For each channel, we assigned the parameterised specparam peaks to canonical bands by their centre frequency. Peak prevalence in a region is the proportion of channels in that region with at least one peak in a given band.


#### Broadband subtraction and recomputed overlap

We reconstructed the fitted aperiodic component on the fitted frequency grid and subtracted it from the empirical PSD in linear power space, giving the residual

$$\mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{osc}}(f) = \mathrm{PSD}(f) - \mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{ap}}(f).$$

This is the primary residual used throughout. We report a log-ratio alternative, $L_{\mathrm{osc}}(f) = \log_{10}(\mathrm{PSD}(f) / \mathrm{PSD}_{\mathrm{ap}}(f))$, which corresponds to the specparam convention, as a sensitivity comparison.

###  Stability of aperiodic estimates

Our last questions asks whether the regional aperiodic estimates agree across three methodological choices. Because some comparisons involve parameters that are not on a common scale, we quantify agreement by correlation, rank-based where the scales differ.


#### Knee vs fixed

For each modality, we compared the channel-level exponent from the knee model with the channel-level exponent from the fixed model. The two exponents are not on the same scale, so the comparison is by Pearson and Spearman rank correlation across channels.

#### Fitting range

For each modality, we computed the fixed-mode exponent over 1-80 Hz and over 1-45 Hz and quantified per-channel agreement between the two estimates.


#### IRASA vs specparam

As a complementary decomposition, we also estimated HD-EEG aperiodic exponents using Irregular Resampling Auto-Spectral Analysis (IRASA; Wen and Liu 2016). IRASA computes the power spectrum at multiple resampling factors ($h = 1.05$ to $2.0$ in steps of $0.05$); for each factor the geometric mean of the up-sampled and down-sampled spectra is taken, and the median across factors gives the fractal (aperiodic) component. Because IRASA up-samples by up to $h_{\max} = 2$, the analysed band is bounded by the Nyquist limit, $h_{\max} \cdot f_{\text{hi}} < f_s / 2$. With $f_s = 200$ Hz this restricts the upper edge to below 50 Hz, so we ran IRASA over 2-40 Hz. We obtained the fractal exponent by fitting a line in log-og space to the IRASA aperiodic spectrum; the sign-reversed slope is the IRASA exponent. For the comparison we refit the specparam fixed-mode exponent over the same 2-40 Hz band and correlated the two across channels (Pearson and Spearman).
